gap: No result ChatGPT got explains that sub-$250 '360°' dash cams use three different mechanisms that change what gets recorded: the 70mai Omni pans one 140° lens with a stepping motor, so it records one direction at a time; the Vantrue E360 stitches two 210° fisheye lenses into one 5184-pixel-wide panorama, which works out to 14.4 px per degree, about the detail of a 1080p camera in any one direction; the Botslab G980H uses four separate cameras.
standout_why: I compared against deal.ai (cited), which lists '70mai Omni 4K 360°' at $250 with '360° field of view' and the E360's '5.2K 360-degree panoramic recording'. It never says how either camera gets to 360°, and its own summary says nothing it found has true 360° coverage. I also compared against Tom's Guide (cited; the fetch returned only navigation, no dash cam text) and Car and Driver's Vantrue deals page (cited; about the N4S, E1 Pro and N5S, not the E360). Neither ChatGPT answer named the E360 at all, though it sells for $139.99 and $209.99 on Vantrue's US store today. The second answer offered 'actual 360° panoramic video, with a rotatable view' as one option, which mixes up a rotating lens and a stitched panorama without explaining either. No page gives pixels per degree or says that a panning lens records only one direction at a time.
decides: If the shopper wants every side recorded at once, this rules out the rotating 70mai Omni: one 140° lens can't record the side it isn't facing. For true panoramic video under $250, the Vantrue E360 ($139.99) or E360 ACE ($209.99, which adds a 2.7K rear camera) is the real candidate. But '5.2K' is the width of the whole 360° image, so each direction gets about the detail of a 1080p camera. For front, rear, left and right with the most detail at the front, the Botslab G980H's separate cameras fit the shopper's words better: about 16.9 px per degree at the front against 14.4 on the E360, by the arithmetic in the findings. Both makers quote 'fields of view' that may be diagonal, so this is a rough comparison, not a measured one. On all three cameras, recording while parked needs a hardwire kit.

findings.note: From Notebookcheck's spec table: 'Dual 210° STARVIS 2 cameras, 2.7k rear camera', video '5184 x 1944 360°'. Arithmetic: 5184 px ÷ 360° = 14.4 horizontal px per degree, so a 140° forward slice gets about 2016 px. A 1080p camera with a 140° lens gives 1920 ÷ 140 = 13.7 px per degree, about the same.

findings.note: I could not open this page myself today: WebFetch returned HTTP 429 three times and storecheck returned HTTP 0. The figures come from Dealectric's own record of this maker page (read 2026-11-21), given in the brief: front 2880 × 1620, rear, left and right 1920 × 1080, all at 25 fps; FOV front 170°, sides 120°, rear 150°. Arithmetic: 2880 ÷ 170 = 16.9; 1920 ÷ 120 = 16.0; 1920 ÷ 150 = 12.8. If the maker's FOV figures are diagonal, the true horizontal density is higher, so this is only a rough comparison.
